summary.text:
The best document we have read, and the one that validated our own engine. Leicestershire published five premature PWLB repayments settled on 31 March 2026 with, for each loan, the principal, coupon, annual interest, premium and premature repayment rate. Almost nobody publishes that.

We ran all five through the canonical break-cost engine. Aggregate premium came out at £3,479,566 against their published £3,470,298 — 0.27% apart. Solving for the discount rate behind each published premium lands within 0.0041 percentage points of the rate they printed to two decimals. The formula agrees exactly; the entire residual is their own rounding. That is the first external check the engine has ever had.

The position itself is unusual. External debt of £130.5m is 'the lowest level for over 20 years', no new loans have been raised since August 2010, and £44.5m was repaid in the year. What remains is £37.0m of PWLB at 8.39% — genuinely historic debt — and £93.5m of market loans at 4.41% with lender options. Investments of £387.5m dwarf the debt and returned 4.69% against a 4.04% average base rate. They are £63m under-borrowed with £388m of cash, and the 2026-2030 programme's £65m of prudential borrowing is expected to be met internally. Two officer addresses are published.

officer.subject: We checked our break-cost engine against your paragraph 24
officer.body:
Hi Declan,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country. So below are a few thoughts ahead of Cabinet on 8 September. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

I want to start with something we owe you, because your annual report did us a favour.

Paragraph 24 publishes all five of the PWLB loans you repaid early on 31 March, loan by loan, with the principal, the coupon, the annual interest, the premium and the premature repayment rate. Almost nobody publishes that last column. It meant we could test our own break-cost engine against a real set of transactions rather than against ourselves.

So we ran them. Our engine returns a total premium of £3,479,566 against your published £3,470,298 — 0.27% apart across the five. Then we solved backwards for the discount rate that would reproduce each of your premiums exactly, and every one came out within 0.0041 percentage points of the rate you printed to two decimals. In other words the formula agrees; the whole difference is the rounding in your own table. That's the first time our engine has been checked against a third party's published numbers, and it's your report that made it possible.

As a second cross-check: we hold all 11 of your remaining PWLB loans, £36.971m at a weighted 8.40%, against the £37.0m at 8.39% in your paragraph 39 table.

On the position itself, there's not much to tell you that you haven't already said better. External debt at £130.5m is the lowest in over twenty years, nothing new has been raised since August 2010, and £388m of cash against £63m of under-borrowing is a comfortable place to be standing. The 2026-2030 programme's £65m of prudential borrowing being met internally follows from that.

The two things that will move on you are both about the curve rather than the balance sheet. The £93.5m of market loans at 4.41% carry lender options, and with ten-year certainty money at 5.83% today the odds on those being exercised aren't what they were when the loans were written. And the remaining £37.0m of PWLB at 8.39% sits at the opposite end: those are the loans where the premium arithmetic changes fastest as gilt yields move, which is exactly the sort of thing worth watching daily rather than at the next quarterly report.

That's what pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis is for — every council's book priced each day against the DMO's repayment curve, same formula you've just seen us reproduce. We never present it as a quote; the DMO's is the binding one. Rates at both fixings are at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard, and the monthly sector breakdown at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity — July was £368m across 33 loans from 19 borrowers, average 5.02%.

On training, three fit Leicestershire: Break costs and premature repayment, given what you've just executed; LOBO loans, for the £93.5m carrying options; and our liability benchmark pathway, which is interactive and built on live data — worth a look given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Codes. For members, Audit Committee Chair (Treasury) is written for exactly the scrutiny your Corporate Governance Committee gives this. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
